Random sampling counters automation bias by ensuring that not all investigations are based solely on high-risk signals from the algorithm. When a random sample is applied, part of the cases is randomly selected for fraud investigation, which encourages inspectors to critically evaluate the outcomes of the algorithm rather than relying on them blindly. This approach helps to mitigate the risk of discrimination by providing a reference point to monitor whether certain groups are disproportionately represented in the algorithm's predictions.

Regarding the AI Act duties for high-risk providers, the use of random sampling is relevant because high-risk AI systems are required to identify and mitigate reasonably foreseeable risks, including potential discrimination. The AI Act mandates that providers of high-risk systems implement measures to ensure compliance with these requirements, and random sampling can serve as a control tool to monitor and address discrimination risks effectively.
